sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces the load and resisting mechanisms and the limit states for soil nail wall design, and a design framework that follows LRFD principles combined with the ASD aspects used in soil nail design software (SNAP-2, Siel 2014). The LRFD resistance factors for each limit state are back-calculated from ASD factors of safety.
sections.body: 5.1 Introduction (p. 97). This chapter introduces the load and resisting mechanisms and the relevant limit states to consider in the design of soil nail walls. It presents a design framework following LRFD principles combined with ASD aspects as used in soil nail design software, SNAP-2 (Siel 2014). Resistance factors used in an LRFD framework for each limit state are back-calculated from ASD factors of safety.

sections.title: Load Transfer Mechanisms
sections.summary: Load transfer during top-down construction (Figure 5.1): the first lift stands unsupported; soil deformation loads the facing, which passes load to the nails and, by shear along the grout-soil interface, to the soil. Nail force rises from the facing to Tmax near the critical slip surface and falls toward the nail end; deeper lifts load lower nails more and may unload upper nails. Nail forces rise up to about 15% after construction (creep, relaxation), covered by bond strength choice. Check intermediate and final stages, including an unsupported lift before nailing (Figure 5.2).
sections.body: 5.2 Load Transfer Mechanisms (pp. 97-99; printed in the body as 'Load Transfer in Soil Nail Walls'). The load-transfer mechanisms from construction to completion: the initial lift height is chosen so that, at the end of Excavation Phase 1 (Figure 5.1), the soil behind the excavation is stable and can remain unsupported before any nails are installed; only soil resistance along potential slip surfaces participates. The upper soil tends to deform outward through Excavation Phase 1, after the first row of nails (Nail 1) and the initial facing are placed; the deformation generates lateral earth pressure on the facing, transferred to the nails and from the nails to the soil by shear mobilized along the grout-soil interface. Axial tensile force T1 develops in Nail 1 and varies with distance x along it: it increases from the facing (x = 0) to a maximum (Tmax) near the critical slip surface for that stage and decreases toward the nail end (x = L). In Excavation Phase 2 the critical slip surface is larger, causing more facing pressure, a larger T1 and larger interface shear, and the location of Tmax moves farther back. After Nail 2 and its facing are installed, further movement transfers more load to Nail 1 and loads Nail 2. Increasing lateral deformation through the last stage (Excavation Phase N) keeps increasing interface shear and axial force in the lowest and intermediate nails, whose maximum force is likely reached at the final excavation phase; loads in upper nails may redistribute and possibly decrease, and stability analyses may show upper nails as ineffective in tension for deep slip surfaces extending behind their ends (Section 5.6), but they remain important for local stability. Nail forces tend to increase moderately, up to approximately 15 percent, after the end of construction, over time and for long-term conditions (Plumelle et al. 1990; Holman and Tuozzolo 2009), mainly due to soil creep and stress relaxation; these increases are not explicit in design but should be considered by selecting bond strengths that account for creep. Design must consider both intermediate and final excavation stages to find the most critical case at each nail level. The critical situation for most designs arises when a combination of loads (dead, live and extreme loads such as earthquake) acts on the wall, but a critical case may also occur after a lift is excavated and before the nails and shotcrete are installed at that level (Figure 5.2), made worse when seepage forces act on the open face.

sections.title: Soil-Nail Interaction and Tensile Force Distribution
sections.summary: Interface shear q is non-uniform and reverses along the nail; the maximum force lies near, not on, the critical slip surface (Figures 5.3, 5.4). Measured maximum forces (Figure 5.5) normalized by Ka gamma_s H SV SH range 0.4-1.1, averaging 0.75 in the upper two thirds: Tmax ~ 0.75 Ka gamma_s H SV SH there, about half that in the lower third. Head force To is smaller (0.50-0.60 Ka gamma_s H SV SH; Figure 5.6); Eq 5.1 (Clouterre 2002) gives To from Tmax and Smax, about 0.7 Tmax at 5 ft. Tmax_i = min(RT, RF, RPO) (Eq 5.2); all nails are designed for the largest Tmax_i.
sections.body: 5.2.1 Soil-Nail Interaction and Tensile Force Distribution (pp. 100-105). 5.2.1a Overview: the interaction between nails, soil and facing is complex and redistributes nail tensile forces; the mobilized grout-soil shear stress q is in general not uniform and changes direction along the nail (Figures 5.3a, b), and the maximum force occurs along the nail (Figure 5.3c). 5.2.1b Maximum Tensile Force Distribution: the force a tendon can develop depends on where it crosses the slip surface; the location of maximum force is close to, but generally does not coincide with, the critical slip surface. Figure 5.4 shows loads and their locations changing from nail to nail; the length Lp behind the slip surface develops pullout resistance, so the upper nail T1 contributes little (small Lp) and T2, T3 more. The maximum force is limited by the tendon tensile strength and by the facing resistances (5.2.1c); soil forces T must not exceed resistances R. Figure 5.5 (full-scale instrumented walls, Byrne et al. 1998): the maximum force in the upper portion occurred about 0.3H to 0.4H behind the facing and in the lower portion about 0.15H to 0.2H behind it. Measured forces normalized by gamma_s, SV, SH, H and Ka represent long-term service forces, excluding frost and earthquake; they range from 0.4 to 1.1, averaging about 0.75 in the upper two thirds, increasing from about 0.5-0.6 near the top to 0.75-0.85 in the central third, decreasing to about 0.4-0.5 in the lower third and 0 at the bottom (consistent with Plumelle et al. 1990; Holman and Tuozzolo 2009). Hence Tmax in the upper two thirds ranges from about 0.50 Ka gamma_s H SV SH to 1.1 Ka gamma_s H SV SH, with an average Tmax = 0.75 Ka gamma_s H SV SH; in the lower third about 50 percent of the upper value. Briaud and Lim (1997) suggested an average Tmax = 0.65 Ka gamma_s H SV SH for the top row and half of this for lower rows, with no cohesion. The average nail force is smaller than one estimated from the full active pressure, so apparent pressure over the tributary area SV x SH may be used to check nail forces routinely calculated by limit equilibrium. 5.2.1c Tensile Forces at the Wall Facing: the nail head force To is smaller than forces along the nail. Figure 5.6 shows working (in-service) normalized head forces, excluding frost: values vary from about 0.6 to 1.0 overall and 0.40 to 0.70 in the upper two thirds (as printed), with an average from To = 0.50 Ka gamma_s H SV SH to 0.60 Ka gamma_s H SV SH, consistent with walls in Germany (Gassler and Gudehus 1981), France (FHWA 1993a) and others (Holman and Tuozzolo 2009); soil arching redistributes load, and closer spacings give smaller head forces than tributary areas suggest. Clouterre (2002) suggested Eq 5.1 for the working head force; for a typical 5-ft spacing To ~ 0.7 Tmax under normal loading and slope; To is limited by the minimum facing resistance. SNAP-2 computes the facing force by Rankine theory and checks it against the resistance (Siel 2014), but Eq 5.1 is preferred in the Chapter 6 procedures. 5.2.1d Considerations for Design: nail tensile load is limited by the minimum of pullout resistance RPO and tendon tensile resistance RT, and at the facing by the minimum facing resistance RF (Figure 5.7); Tmax_i, from limit-equilibrium analyses, is given by Eq 5.2: pullout controls if RPO is least, tension if RT is least (printed 'RT < RP and RF'), facing controls To if RF is least. Limit-equilibrium analyses cannot reproduce the actual deformation and load mobilization of this top-down system, and loads vary greatly with nail layout even for layouts with the same overall factor of safety (Chapter 6). Usually all nails have the same RT and RF but different pullout resistance because Lp differs (Point A in Figure 5.7). All nails are designed for Tmax, the maximum Tmax_i of all nails, so other rows are over-designed for the critical slip surface but matter for other surfaces and stages; optimizing individual nails is rarely done.

sections.title: Design Framework
sections.summary: The manual's framework takes account of ASD factors of safety and integrates LRFD principles. Because LRFD-based slope stability procedures are not available, ASD-based stability calculations quantify loads and slip geometries, and those values are then used in limit state checks (5.3.1 to 5.3.4).
sections.body: 5.3 Design Framework (pp. 106-107; printed in the body as 'Introduction to Design Framework'). The manual introduces a framework that (i) takes into account factors of safety (FS) as previously used in ASD and (ii) integrates LRFD principles. Soil nail design was previously completed with ASD and limit-equilibrium slope stability analyses; designers today are limited to ASD-based slope stability procedures because LRFD-based ones are not available. A soil nail wall design must therefore use ASD-based stability calculations to quantify loads and slip plane geometries, then use those values to perform limit state checks. Subsections 5.3.1 to 5.3.4.
key_points: Framework combines ASD factors of safety with LRFD principles
No LRFD slope stability procedures exist; ASD stability analyses give loads and slip geometry
Limit state checks then made on those values

sections.title: Use of LRFD and ASD Platforms
sections.summary: Structural resistances are verified in LRFD format with AASHTO (2014) load factors and results of ASD-based stability analysis. The resistance factors were derived to relate to AASHTO (2014) load factors, be compatible with (not necessarily equal to) AASHTO factors for comparable structures, relate to the previous manual's FS where applicable, and be consistent with the minimum frequency of verification load testing.
sections.body: 5.3.1 Use of LRFD and ASD Platforms (p. 107). The manual presents a procedure to verify structural resistances in an LRFD format using AASHTO (2014) load factors and results from ASD-based slope stability analysis. The LRFD resistance factors were derived to be: (i) related to AASHTO (2014) load factors; (ii) compatible with (but not necessarily equal to) those in AASHTO (2014) for comparable structures; (iii) related to FS in the previous version of the manual, where applicable, to fit past practice until new research emerges; and (iv) consistent with the minimum required frequency of verification load testing.

sections.title: Allowable Stress Design (ASD)
sections.summary: ASD design condition: sum of load effects <= Rall = Rn/FS (Eq 5.3), with one FS for all uncertainty. Table 5.1 gives minimum FS (same as the previous edition): overall stability 1.5 static (1.35 for some non-critical permanent walls), 1.1 seismic; excavation short term 1.25-1.33; basal heave 2.0 short, 2.5 long term (2.3 seismic); pullout 2.0/1.5; lateral sliding 1.5/1.1; tendon Grades 60 and 75 1.8/1.35, Grades 95 and 150 2.0/1.50; facing flexure and punching 1.5/1.1; headed studs A307 2.0/1.5, A325 1.7/1.3.
sections.body: 5.3.2 Allowable Stress Design (ASD) (pp. 107-108). The ASD design condition is Eq 5.3: the effect of all combined loads on a component in a given limit state, sum(Qi), must not exceed the allowable value Rall = Rn/FS, where Rn is the ultimate capacity and FS the single factor accounting for all design, material and construction uncertainty; allowable values represent working conditions. Table 5.1 gives minimum recommended factors of safety (static / seismic), the same as the previous edition: overall stability FSOS 1.5 (note 2: some Owners may accept 1.35 for non-critical permanent structures with sufficient geotechnical information and successful local experience) / 1.1 (note 6: 1.0 when horizontal seismic coefficients are derived from estimated allowable seismic deformations); overall, short-term excavation condition FSOS 1.25-1.33 (temporary lifts unsupported up to 2 days; larger value for critical structures or more uncertain soils) / NA; basal heave FSBH 2.0 (permanent walls, short term) and 2.5 (permanent walls, long term) / 2.3; pullout FSPO 2.0 / 1.5; lateral sliding FSLS 1.5 / 1.1; tendon tensile strength FST 1.8 / 1.35 (Grades 60 and 75) and 2.0 / 1.50 (Grades 95 and 150); facing flexural FSFF 1.5 / 1.1; facing punching shear FSFP 1.5 / 1.1; headed stud tensile FSFH 2.0 / 1.5 (A307 bolt) and 1.7 / 1.3 (A325 bolt). Note 1: limit state and symbol nomenclature differ from the previous manual, reflecting LRFD terminology in AASHTO (2014).

sections.title: Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD)
sections.summary: ASD slope stability results must be checked with LRFD procedures for all limit states: phi Rn >= sum(gamma_i eta_i Qi) (Eq 5.4), eta_i = 1.0 for soil nail walls. Nominal resistance equals strength; for soils it is a mean value. Load factors come from AASHTO (2014), which has no soil nail resistance factors; the manual's are given per limit state. Capacity-to-demand ratio CDR = phi Rn / sum(gamma_i Qi) >= 1.0 (Eq 5.5).
sections.body: 5.3.3 Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) (pp. 109-110). Transportation structures are designed on an LRFD platform; ASD slope stability results must be checked with LRFD procedures, verifying that no limit state is exceeded. The LRFD condition is Eq 5.4, with Rn the nominal resistance of a component for a limit state, phi its resistance factor, Qi a load or effect, gamma_i its load factor and eta_i the load modification factor for ductility, redundancy or operational classification (equal to 1.0 for soil nail walls). Nominal resistances include tendon yield strength, nail pullout resistance, soil shear strength and facing resistances; 'strength' (ASD) is equivalent to 'nominal resistance' (LRFD). Nominal resistances of soils and other natural materials are mean values, obtained by the Chapter 4 methods. Load factors are defined in AASHTO (2014), but resistance factors for soil nail walls are not; the manual gives them per mechanism and limit state. The objective is a factored resistance greater than the factored load, quantified by the capacity-to-demand ratio CDR (Eq 5.5).
key_points: Eq 5.4: phi Rn >= sum(gamma_i eta_i Qi), eta_i = 1.0 for soil nail walls

sections.title: Calibration of Resistance Factors
sections.summary: A reliability calibration for pullout (NCHRP Report 701, Lazarte 2011) was only preliminary because load test data were inconsistent and many tests did not reach maximum pullout. The manual's resistance factors were back-calibrated from Table 5.1's FS. Pullout factors are valid only with proof tests on at least 5% of production nails and project-specific verification tests (more for more soil types, variability, larger walls; Chapter 9). Using ASD programs with back-calibrated factors is interim.
sections.body: 5.3.4 Calibration of Resistance Factors (pp. 110-111). The most advanced calibration methods use reliable statistical data and adequate methods for acceptable reliability, but consistent and complete soil nail databases are limited (NCHRP Report 701, Lazarte 2011). That research calibrated a pullout resistance factor from a load test database; data inconsistencies, incomplete installation information and poor documentation, and above all tests that did not apply enough force to reach the expected maximum pullout resistance, meant only a preliminary reliability-based set of pullout factors. The manual's resistance factors were back-calibrated from the safety factors in Table 5.1, with the basis given for each limit state; this allows LRFD verifications or designs with existing ASD slope stability procedures. The factors are valid for a minimum frequency of load testing in a performance monitoring program (Chapter 9): pullout factors are valid as long as proof load tests are conducted during construction on a minimum of 5 percent of the total production nails; the number of verification tests is project-specific, with more for (i) more soil types behind the wall, (ii) higher property variability even in one soil, and (iii) larger and longer walls. Using ASD-based programs with factors calibrated from FS is an interim provision; one limitation is that ASD programs cannot apply different load factors to different load components.

sections.body: 5.4.2 Load Factors (pp. 111-113). The combinations include permanent, transient and extreme-event loads, with factors from AASHTO (2014) Tables 3.4.1-1 and 3.4.1-2. Permanent loads for earth-retaining structures may include DC (dead loads of structural components and attachments), DW (wearing surfaces and utilities, when supporting a bridge abutment or roadway), EH (horizontal earth pressure), ES (earth surcharge) and EV (vertical pressure from earth fill dead load); EH and EV are treated differently from other earth-retaining structures because of soil nail software limitations (Section 5.6). Transient loads may include vehicular live load (LL), live load surcharge (LS), construction equipment and other live surcharge, including equipment in intermediate stages; superstructure loads may reach an abutment (AASHTO 2014 Article 3.11.6.4), but soil nail walls supporting bridges are outside the manual's scope, and abutment wall settlement may need consideration in bridge design. Extreme-event loads are earthquake (EQ; Section 6.8). Table 5.2 (AASHTO 2014): Strength I, permanent gamma_p (Table 5.3), transient 1.75, extreme NA; Extreme Event I, gamma_p, NA, 1.00; Service I, 1.00, 1.00, 1.00; only permanent and extreme-event factors are used in the manual's verifications. gamma_p takes the maximum when a load destabilizes and the minimum when it stabilizes (AASHTO 2014 Article 3.4.1). Table 5.3 (maximum / minimum): DC 1.25 / 0.90; DW 1.50 / 0.65; EH active 1.50 / 0.90; EH at-rest 1.35 / 0.90; EV overall stability 1.00 / N/A; EV retaining walls and abutments 1.35 / 1.00 (used in the manual primarily for static loads); ES 1.50 / 0.75. Because ASD programs cannot handle separate load factors, only the maximum vertical earth load factor, gamma_EV = 1.35, is used for static LRFD verifications, justified by model-wall analyses showing vertical earth load effects larger than horizontal; an interim provision. Service load factors are 1.0 for all loads: overall stability (Section 5.6) and deformation (Section 5.9) use Service I with unfactored loads, overall stability being treated as a service limit state for lack of compatible LRFD limit-equilibrium methods. To apply different factors to loads other than soil weight (surcharge, traffic) in an ASD program, enter each such load as its value times gamma/gamma_EV.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Overall stability is checked for internal stability (soil and nails contribute) and global stability (as defined here, no nail contribution), and may include special conditions such as basal heave.
sections.body: 5.6.1 Overview (p. 116). Overall stability of soil nail walls is analyzed and checked for internal and global stability. Internal stability involves contributions from both the soil and the nails; global stability (as defined herein) involves no contribution from the nails. Overall stability may also cover special conditions such as basal heave.
key_points: Internal stability: soil and nails contribute
Global stability (as defined here): no nail contribution
Special cases such as basal heave
sections.applicability: Definitions of internal and global stability.

sections.title: Internal Stability
sections.summary: Slip surfaces through soil and some or all nails; nail pullout behind the surface contributes (tension is checked separately, 5.8.1). Evaluated by 2-D limit equilibrium for the lowest FS; surface shape (planar, bilinear, parabolic, log spiral, circular) matters little if exits are similar. Programs: SNAIL, SNAILZ, GoldNail, SNAP-2 (only one checking the facing), SNAIL Plus; Slope/W, XSTABL, Slide. Allowable bond = bond strength x 1/FSPO. Limit equilibrium puts the largest nail forces low on the wall, unlike measurements; shorten lower nails.
sections.body: 5.6.2 Internal Stability (pp. 116-118). Internal stability must be considered for slip surfaces through the soil and some or all of the nails; soil strength may be frictional, cohesive or both depending on soil type and whether loading is drained or undrained. Where the surface intersects nails, the mobilized pullout resistance behind it contributes; nail tensile resistance is treated separately as a structural limit state (Section 5.8.1). Internal stability is routinely evaluated with two-dimensional limit-equilibrium analyses as in conventional ASD slope stability: many surfaces are analyzed for the lowest FS, which must equal or exceed the minimum acceptable FS, and the analysis gives the critical slip surface and the nail tensile forces. Procedures consider planar (Sheahan and Oral 2002), bilinear (Stocker et al. 1979; Caltrans 1991), parabolic (Shen et al. 1981), log spiral (Christopher et al. 1990) and circular (Golder 1993; Siel 2014) surfaces; the shape generally does not significantly affect the FS (Long et al. 1990) if surfaces exit in front of the wall and behind it at about the same locations. Analyses are most commonly done with dedicated programs: SNAIL (Caltrans 1991), SNAILZ (Caltrans 2007), GoldNail (Golder 1993) and FHWA's SNAP-2 (Siel 2014); of these only SNAP-2 checks facing strengths. Any may be used if the user understands how parameters are used; others include the updated SNAIL and the commercial SNAIL Plus. General programs such as Slope/W (Geostudio 2012), XSTABL (Softpile 2013) or Slide 6.0 (Rocscience 2013) can model multi-level generic reinforcement but are cumbersome for design scenarios; they may be needed to verify global stability, which most dedicated programs cannot address correctly. Minimum safety factors (Table 5.1) are entered into ASD programs; e.g., SNAILZ and GoldNail use allowable bond stresses equal to the bond strength times a user reduction factor equal to 1/FSPO; preliminary dimensions and tendon yield strength are entered as a trial design. Limit-equilibrium programs cannot reproduce actual nail force distributions: measured walls (Section 5.2.1b) show the largest forces in the upper two thirds, a result of top-down staged construction, while limit-equilibrium programs tend to predict larger forces near the bottom (at least for homogeneous conditions and uniform lengths), considering equilibrium but ignoring kinematics and deformation. They yield safe designs meeting the minimum stability criteria (printed cross-reference 'Section 6.6.3 Resistance Factors for Overall Stability'; the heading of that title in this chapter is 5.6.5) but nail force distributions that may not be optimal for limiting deformation near the top, or larger than actual loads. A simple counter is to make nails in the lower half increasingly shorter toward the bottom (Section 6.3.3e).

sections.title: Global Stability
sections.summary: Global stability (2-D limit equilibrium, ASD) is better done with general slope stability programs: SNAIL and SNAILZ treat resistance under the toe by a simple passive approach, GoldNail passes surfaces only through the toe, while SNAP-2 lets surfaces pass above, at or below the toe with proper limit-equilibrium resistance (used for Appendix C). Minimum FS are similar to internal stability; special cases are basal heave (5.6.6) and lateral sliding (5.7.3).
sections.body: 5.6.3 Global Stability (p. 118). Global stability is also routinely evaluated with two-dimensional limit-equilibrium analyses in an ASD framework, more adequately with general slope stability programs than with dedicated soil nail software, most of which has limitations. Slip surfaces in SNAIL and SNAILZ extend under the toe, but the programs estimate resistance under the toe by a simple passive approach; in GoldNail surfaces pass only through the toe; in SNAP-2 surfaces can pass above, at or under the toe and the resistance under the toe uses an appropriate limit-equilibrium formulation. The Appendix C design example uses SNAP-2. Minimum safety factors for global stability are similar to those for internal stability; special cases are Section 5.6.6 'Basal Heave' and Section 5.7.3 'Lateral Sliding Stability.'
key_points: Global stability better analyzed with general slope stability programs
SNAIL/SNAILZ: simple passive resistance under the toe; GoldNail: surfaces only through the toe
SNAP-2: surfaces above, at or below the toe with limit-equilibrium resistance (Appendix C example)
Minimum FS similar to internal stability; basal heave and lateral sliding are special cases

sections.title: Idealized Example
sections.summary: A manual check of a single-nail wall with a planar wedge (Figure 5.9) to illustrate the forces; hand calculations are rare and serve to spot-check software. Factored resistance phi[(W+Q) cos alpha + T sin beta] tan phi_s (Eq 5.6) equals factored driving force gamma (W+Q) sin alpha - T cos beta (Eq 5.7), giving the mobilized T (Eq 5.8); the ASD form (Eq 5.9) uses FS. Overall stability is checked at Service I (gamma = 1.0), where phi is about 1/FS.
sections.body: 5.6.4 Idealized Example (pp. 118-120). A manual check of internal stability illustrates the interaction of forces; manual calculations for complete design are rarely performed but can spot-check computer results; LRFD and ASD checks are shown. Figure 5.9: a generic single-nail wall of height H; the nail is inclined i from horizontal; the slip surface is a plane inclined alpha from horizontal defining a wedge, at angle beta to the nail. T is mobilized up to its nominal pullout resistance behind the slip surface; loads are an external surcharge Q and the wedge weight W; RS is the resultant nominal soil resistance; the soil is purely frictional; for simplicity Q and W take the same load factor. Taking components parallel to the slip plane, the factored resistance from the normal components of W, Q and T is Eq 5.6, with phi the resistance factor for soil strength, N the normal force and phi_s the ultimate friction angle. The parallel component of T is treated as a driving force (it could also be factored); the factored driving force is Eq 5.7. Equilibrium (factored driving force = factored resistance) gives T (Eq 5.8), from which the nail length and section and facing characteristics may be developed. In ASD the frictional resistance is reduced to N tan phi_s/FS and loads are unfactored, giving Eq 5.9. Overall stability should be investigated at the Service I combination with an appropriate resistance factor; with gamma = 1.0 for permanent loads, comparing Eqs 5.8 and 5.9 shows phi approximately equal to 1/FS. Real slip surfaces are more complex and hand analysis is impractical; programs do it efficiently, and back-calibrating a resistance factor from FS once the load factor is defined still applies.
key_points: Hand checks are rare; use them to spot-check software

sections.title: Basal Heave
sections.summary: Evaluate basal heave where soft fine-grained soils lie beneath the excavation (uncommon for soil nail walls). AASHTO (2014) 11.9.5.2 commentary: heave may occur for Su < 0.15 gamma_s' H. Resistance RS = Su Nc B'e or Su Nc DB (Eqs 5.10, 5.11), B'e ~ 0.707 Be, Nc from Figure 5.11 (5.14 conservatively for long, wide excavations); base pressure q (Eq 5.12); check phi_BH 5.14 Su >= gamma_EV q (Eqs 5.13-5.15), gamma_EV = 1.35. Table 5.5: phi_BH = 0.65 short term, 0.50 long term. Lateral squeeze is a variation, not presented.
sections.body: 5.6.6 Basal Heave (pp. 121-125). 5.6.6a Methodology: evaluate basal heave where soft, fine-grained soils lie beneath the excavation (Figure 5.8c); an excessive excavation depth may cause the bottom to heave. It is uncommon for soil nail walls, which are rarely built over or in soft fine-grained soils, but the check allows a feasibility evaluation. AASHTO (2014) Article 11.9.3 commentary guides anchored walls and may be applied to other top-down construction; Section 11.9.5.2 commentary indicates heave may occur under a wall in or over soft clays with Su < 0.15 gamma_s' H (gamma_s' buoyant unit weight, H wall height), and such a wall should be embedded. Soil nail walls over soft clays are more susceptible than embedded systems because most nails are not embedded below the toe; an alternative support system may be necessary if the potential is significant. If the excavation is entirely in fine-grained soils, the nominal resistance RS develops along a composite slip surface (Figure 5.10); width B'e depends on the excavation width Be (ideally without nail influence) or a stiff layer within depth DB. RS (force per linear foot) is Su Nc B'e if B'e < DB (Eq 5.10) or Su Nc DB if B'e >= DB (Eq 5.11), with Su the undrained strength below the wall, Nc the cohesion factor (Figure 5.11), B'e ~ 0.707 Be and DB the depth to stiff soil. Nail contribution is disregarded (nails are particularly inefficient for this limit state). Nc depends on H/Be and Be/Le (excavation height, width, length); for very long walls (Be/Le ~ 0) and very wide excavations (H/Be ~ 0), Nc = 5.14 conservatively. The total pressure at the base of the block is Eq 5.12, with Qi total load at the block base, gamma_s unit weight behind the wall, Q external dead or live load, and Su1 the undrained strength of the soil behind the block (not factored, as a simplification that appears neutral); if B'e >= DB, DB replaces B'e. Stability: Eq 5.13 with phi_BH the resistance factor and gamma_EV = 1.35 (Table 5.3). Disregarding the shear resistance behind the wall (Terzaghi), heave will not occur if Eq 5.14 holds (printed with a minus sign before Q/B'e, while Eq 5.12 adds Q; DB replaces B'e if B'e >= DB), and with Q = 0 if Eq 5.15 holds. 5.6.6b Resistance Factors for Basal Heave: rewriting Eq 5.15 as Eq 5.16 (FS = 5.14 Su / (H gamma_s) = gamma_EV / phi_BH) and fitting the minimum FS of 2.0 (short term) and 2.5 (long term) from Table 5.1 gives Table 5.5: permanent wall short term phi_BH = 0.65, long term phi_BH = 0.50. 5.6.6c Lateral Squeeze: abutment walls over soft soils under unbalanced embankment load may squeeze laterally, a service limit state controlled by deformation; it is not presented, being considered a variation of basal heave (both controlled by low strength and high compressibility of fine-grained soils).

sections.title: Lateral Sliding Stability
sections.summary: Lateral sliding, a special case of global stability, may occur over a weak layer beneath the reinforced block with no nail contribution; check with a general slope program or as a rigid block (Figure 5.12) at Strength I: phi_LS Rs >= gamma_EH Pa cos delta + gamma_ES ES (Eq 5.17), Rs = cb BL + (W + Pa sin delta) tan phi'_fb (Eq 5.18), Pa = gamma_s H1^2 Ka / 2 (Eqs 5.19, 5.20), Ka by Coulomb or Rankine (Eqs 5.21-5.23); gamma_EH = gamma_ES = 1.50. Use fully softened or residual strength on fissured clays. Table 5.7: phi_LS 1.00 static, 0.90 seismic.
sections.body: 5.7.3 Lateral Sliding Stability (pp. 126-131). 5.7.3a Methodology: lateral sliding is not present in most designs but is a special case of global stability that may arise when a weak layer underlies the reinforced block (Figure 5.8d) and nails do not contribute. It can be checked with a general slope program forcing slip surfaces along the weak layer (soil nail programs generally cannot model horizontal segments), or like sliding of a gravity structure by a simplified manual procedure that also illustrates LRFD. The wall is a rigid block loaded by a generally non-horizontal earth pressure acting beyond the longest nail (no nail contribution), with a permanent earth surcharge QES behind it whose horizontal effect is ES (Figure 5.12). The case is Strength I; lateral loads by Coulomb or Rankine theory (AASHTO 2014 Article 3.11.5.1). The horizontal earth load EH is Pa cos delta, with Pa the lateral thrust and delta the friction angle between the block and retained soil, typically the soil friction angle but possibly taken equal to the backslope inclination beta_eq if safe. Check Eq 5.17, with phi_LS the resistance factor, Rs the nominal base resistance per unit width, gamma_EH = 1.5 the maximum load factor for horizontal earth loads (printed 'from Table 5.3 for Strength I, and Table 5.3 for permanent loads, active conditions'), gamma_ES = 1.50 for the horizontal surcharge effect ES. Rs by Eq 5.18, with cb the effective cohesion along the base, BL the length of the horizontal slip surface where cb acts, W the reinforced mass weight and phi'_fb the effective base friction angle (remolded or residual values may apply); W and Pa sin delta implicitly carry the minimum gamma_EV = 1.00, and the vertical effect of QES is omitted for simplicity. The active thrust per unit width is Eq 5.19 over the effective height H1 (Eq 5.20; alpha face batter angle). With no slope break within 2H of the wall the slope is infinite and beta_eq = beta; with a break within 2H, beta_eq = tan^-1(Delta H / 2H), Delta H the rise over 2H. Ka for cohesionless retained soil by Coulomb (Eq 5.21; phi_f friction angle of the retained soil, theta = alpha + 90 degrees the inclination of the back of the facing), more general than Rankine; for walls with alpha < 8 degrees, Rankine (Eq 5.22); for a vertical wall, horizontal ground and delta = 0, Eq 5.23. Where sliding occurs along stiff fissured clays, use the fully softened strength for phi_f, or the residual strength if significant shearing and displacement have occurred along the base. 5.7.3b Resistance Factors for Lateral Sliding: back-calibrated from ASD safety factors with maximum load factors 1.50 for EH and ES and minimum 1.0 for EV (Table 5.3): Table 5.7, static phi_LS = 1.00, seismic phi_LS = 0.90.

sections.title: Overview of Facing Limit States
sections.summary: Facing-nail head limit states (Figure 5.13): bending/flexure, considered separately for initial and final facings (initial facing disregarded in final facing design); punching shear around the nails, separately for each facing; and headed stud tension, final facing only. Facing and nail head hardware must give resistances exceeding the maximum head force To.
sections.body: 5.8.2 Overview of Facing Limit States (pp. 131-132). The strength limit states at the facing-nail head connection (Figure 5.13): Bending/Flexure, when the facing moment exceeds its resistance, considered separately for initial and final facings, the initial facing being disregarded in the design of the final facing (Figure 5.13b); Punching Shear, in the facing around the nails, evaluated separately for initial and final facings (Figures 5.13c, d); and Headed Stud Tensile, when the stud tensile resistance is exceeded, final facing only (Figure 5.13e). The facing and nail head elements must provide resistance in excess of the maximum nail head force To for each limit state, with appropriate facing dimensions, strength and reinforcement and suitable hardware (bearing plate, nut, headed studs).

sections.title: Facing Flexural Strength Limit State
sections.summary: The facing is a continuous two-way slab supported by the nails; flexure fails by yield lines (Figure 5.14), positive moments between nails and negative around them, vertical (mV) and horizontal (mH) moments. Resistance by reinforced concrete formulas with steel at mid-thickness (Figure 5.15): c = 0.85 f'c a, t = fy_W as_eq, equivalent rebar area (Eqs 5.24-5.28), mv = as_eq fy_W (hi/2 - as_eq fy_W / 1.7 f'c) (Eq 5.29), at nail heads and mid-span in both directions. sections.body: 5.8.3 Facing Flexural Strength Limit State (pp. 132-139). 5.8.3a Introduction: lateral earth pressures cause bending in the facing, considered a continuous two-way slab supported by the nails; the limit state is reached when increasing pressure produces a yielding mechanism (yield lines across the slab, Figure 5.14). Moments produce tension on the outside between nails (positive) and on the inside around the nails (negative), about horizontal axes (vertical moments mV, Figure 5.13b) and vertical axes (horizontal moments mH). Maximum moments depend on SH and SV, initial and final facing thicknesses hi and hf, reinforcement layout, type and strength (WWM and any rebar) and shotcrete/concrete resistance (Seible 1996). 5.8.3b Bending Mechanisms: resistances follow conventional reinforced concrete formulas for a section of thickness hi (or hf) with reinforcement (WWM alone or with rebar) at mid-section (Figure 5.15); mv acts about a horizontal axis and generates a compressive force c over the compression extent a and a tensile force per unit length t; d is the distance from the compression edge to the tension steel centroid, with di and df half of hi and hf. Nominal compressive resistance Eq 5.24 (f'c shotcrete or concrete strength; a extent of compression, uniform stress assumed); SH may be taken as the section width but forces and moments are per unit length. Nominal tensile resistance Eq 5.25 (fy_W WWM yield strength, assumed primary; as_eq equivalent area per unit width), more generally Eq 5.26 with WWM area per unit width as_W, rebar yield strength fy_R, rebar area As_R and S = SH or SV. Equivalent rebar area for different yield strengths, Eq 5.27, and total equivalent area per unit length, Eq 5.28 (as printed, Eq 5.27 already divides As_R by S and Eq 5.28 divides A's_R by S again). Force equilibrium (c = t) and moment equilibrium (mv = t z, z = d - a/2) give Eq 5.29 (the text prints 'hi = di/2'; the definition above makes di half of hi). All reinforcement is assumed to yield and its centroid in each direction to be at mid-section; Eq 5.29 is used in Chapter 6. Moments must be evaluated around the nail heads and in the span between nails, in both directions; commonly WWM plus rebar around nail heads and WWM only in the span of the initial facing, and rebar only, both ways, in the final facing (Chapter 3). 5.8.3c Resistance Factors for Flexure at Facing: back-calibrated with gamma_EV = 1.35 static and 1.00 seismic; Table 5.9: initial and final facing, phi_FF = 0.90 static and 0.90 seismic.

sections.summary: Most movement in granular soils occurs during or shortly after excavation; maximum horizontal movement at the top; settlement of similar order. Long-term top movement delta_v ~ delta_h = (delta_h/H)i H (Eq 5.30, Clouterre 1991), valid for L/H >= 0.7, negligible surcharge, FSOS >= 1.5; Table 5.12: (delta_h/H)i 1/1000, 1/500, 1/333 and C 0.8, 1.25, 1.5 (weathered rock and stiff soil, sand, fine-grained). sections.body: 5.9.2 Soil Nail Wall Displacements (pp. 140-142). A soil nail wall is a passive system and some deformation should be expected; the wall and soil deform outward during and after construction. In predominantly granular soils most movement occurs during or shortly after excavation, and post-construction movement is generally small unless the wall, its foundation or the retained soil deteriorates; creep of retained fine-grained soils may raise nail forces and wall deflection after construction. Maximum horizontal displacements commonly occur at the top; settlements are generally small and of the same order as the horizontal top movement. Lateral deflections are larger for taller walls and increasing nail spacing, inclination and surcharge, and smaller with more wall batter, stiffer soil or closer nail spacing; vertical displacements depend on similar factors, are largest near the facing and commonly smaller than the lateral top deflection. The maximum long-term horizontal and vertical top displacements delta_h and delta_v (printed 'Figure 5.20'; the deformation figure is Figure 5.16) may be estimated by Eq 5.30 (Clouterre 1991), valid for (i) L/H >= 0.7 (L nail length, H wall height), (ii) negligible surcharge and (iii) FSOS >= 1.5. Table 5.12 (modified from Clouterre 1993 and Byrne et al. 1998): (delta_h/H)i = 1/1000 weathered rock and stiff soil, 1/500 sandy soil, 1/333 fine-grained soil; C = 0.8, 1.25, 1.5. Ground deformation can be significant up to DDEF behind the wall (Eq 5.31; alpha wall batter angle, C from Table 5.12). Where critical or sensitive structures are nearby, a project-specific assessment of wall movement effects is warranted, by numerical methods and/or data from similar walls in similar ground. Horizontal deflections greater than 0.005H during construction should be a cause for concern, as they generally represent an upper limit of acceptable performance. Deformations may be mitigated by battering the wall, longer nails in the upper portion, more nail steel per unit wall area, or in some cases ground anchors with the nails. Monitoring shows movement can continue after construction, sometimes up to 6 months, longer in soils with creep potential; long-term deformation may increase up to 15 percent beyond that observed soon after construction, adding nail tension. High plasticity fine-grained soils (approximately PI > 20) with high water contents (LI > 0.2) tend to deform for longer due to creep.
